summary: Parallel readers map the full level-design history of Oma's Mahjong: what was tried, what failed, why, and what tools exist

result.area: Codex tasks 1-6 (level factory for 200-225, 2026-11-04 to 2026-11-05) and their results
result.summary:
Tasks 1-6 ran over about 25 hours (2026-11-04 to 2026-11-05 23:40). They are the "random deals with traps bolted on, then hit the numbers" phase of the 200-225 batch. The factory, Codex's code adopted by Claude as wip/level-factory, works like this: build fresh original whole layouts, author a recipe (named trap combinations such as clockOnTopLocked or keysAcross+frozenGuards) onto many seeded deals, make variants (mostly "reveal/hide N covered pictures" and "clock spare N"), and rate every variant with the family bot human-g6.2. The rating is two fixed seeds (4711 and 18427), 40 campaigns each, with a 20-try cap. A skilled "planner" bot then runs the quality gates, and a branch-and-bound assignment puts boards into slots.

Task 01 (curve 7 at 200, 9 at 224, 10 at 225) gave 15/26. That came from a pool of 2,100 candidates, 273 full two-seed ratings and 58 quality passes. 222 of the 273 missed their slot by more than 0.5 and 48 had seeds more than 2 tries apart. Claude found a winner's curse in tuning, so a fresh seed (29717) was added for tuned rows. Task 02 (fill the 11 gaps) was superseded within 10 minutes. Dennis played round 1 and said "the first levels are too easy. Start the levels at 10 tries at 200". Task 03 moved the curve to family 10 at 200, 12 at 224, 13 at 225, added skilled at least 2.5 (Dennis: "require the skilled bot to at least need 2.5-3 tries"), a 72-tile minimum and discouraged block shapes. Only one round-1 board still fit: the old 225 moved to slot 201.

Task 04 fixed a skilled-bot blind spot (locked/frozen clocks with keys across the pile; the 212 board went 11.7 to 2.15). Tasks 03 and 04 gave 13/26 from 4,231 candidates, 777 full ratings and 47 quality passes. Dennis's round-2 lab verdicts and quotes then drove Task 05. Its points: spare 1 on tray-juggle levels, and smarter trap placement from a 0-100 score built on his comments (trap early to middle, specials show the way, no blind digging, a fair clock that matters, a temptation, pile shapes rather than blobs). Task 05 also brought another skilled bot (better of two styles). It produced 132 new deals with mean placement score 86, and zero new qualifiers. The new bot knocked 4 of the 13 accepted boards (210, 217, 220, 225) under the 2.5 skilled floor, so v11 is 9/26. Codex said the placement score "did not predict expert challenge". The main failure became "skilled too easy": boards the family needs 10-12 tries for, the skilled bot clears in about 1.0-1.15.

Task 06 (close the family/skilled gap: let Dennis's own lab tries stand in for the skilled rating, fit a skilled predictor, explain the 201 face-up oddity) was superseded before it ran. At 23:27 Dennis said he does not want to playtest routinely and asked for "tiny puzzle pieces / traps ... knowing how hard the outcoming level generally will be". That became Task 07 (v12 is in fact Task 07's handback).

My own read-only analysis of the handed-back pools found four things:
- Family and skilled ratings are essentially uncorrelated: r = 0.16 (round 1), -0.04 (v10), -0.33 (v11).
- Seed-to-seed agreement on one board is only r = 0.71-0.83, with a median gap of about 1 try. 16-21% of boards differ by more than 2 tries.
- A recipe's family rating spreads across about 4-6 tries between its quartiles.
- Only 2 of 15 (round 1) and 2 of 13 (v10) delivered boards ended up in the slot they were authored for. Slots were filled by over-producing and assigning, not by design.

The steering journal (624 measured edits) shows that almost no edit has a reliable direction. Even the "reliable" ones Claude told Codex to prefer (the luck moment, one ice softer) have a median effect of about x1.0, and 253 of 624 edits moved the rating by 3 tries or more.

keyFacts.fact: TASK-01 (2026-11-04): Codex runs production for 200-225 only on Dennis's PC (run_original.js, 4 construction workers, 6 bot workers, 8 deals per layout), then tunes near-misses that are within 2.5 tries but not within 0.5, includes Claude's 9 cloud-tuned v7/v8 rows, then assigns, verifies and previews. Curve: 200 at 7 family tries, 224 at 9, 225 at 10; big boards only at 210 and 220.

Task 01 qualification gates (called Dennis's decisions): family rating = pooled mean of seeds 4711 and 18427 (40 campaigns each, 20-try cap) within 0.5 of target; seeds within 2 tries; skilled planner <= 6; at most 1 unrelieved blind dig; losses at the traps >= 60%; every special matters (removing it changes the family rating); clock spare 1-3; the 'don't grab the clock first' check must show at least 1 try worse; original layouts (D4 overlap < 75%, no crops or derived boards, max 3 of one recipe); late squeeze is only a warning.

Task 01 23:00 update: Claude found the tuning holdout was not independent (tuning pooled 4711+18427 and the holdout was 18427 again: a winner's curse; two seeds agree only r=0.74 across boards). From then on, tuned rows must also land within 0.5 on a fresh seed 29717. Claude also passed on 'lessons' from 101 moves: a luck moment is the reliable harder step; adding traps makes boards EASIER (deepKeys x0.48, lockedPartners x0.31); one spare less x1.65 is a cliff; one ice softer or half the ice x0.82-0.84.

Task 01 result: 15/26 qualified (missing 207, 208, 209, 210, 213, 214, 215, 216, 218, 221, 222). Pool 2,100; screened 1,864; full two-seed ratings 273; quality checks 96; quality passes 58. 222 of 273 missed the slot target by more than 0.5; 48 had seed gaps above 2. Quality failure reasons: clock-first lesson 15, idle ice 13, plannerScreen 6, skilled > 6 4. Assignment hit its 3M-node limit with a relaxed upper bound of 16 slots.
Round-1 skilled ratings were very low against family 7-10: 200 skilled 1.0, 212 1.05, 217 1.02, 224 1.02, 204 1.45. Only 225 (70bde28d4c0922c5) had skilled 5.42. There was no skilled floor yet.
Single-seed noise is large. Round-1 213 pooled 8.015 (7.03/9.00) but fresh seed 10.53. Round-1 222 seeds 8.1/10.13. v10 221 seeds 8.47/15.05. v12 217 candidate seeds 8.20/14.63/14.28.

Codex's rule critique (Task 01): the half-try band creates sharp edges. Near misses of 0.51, 0.505 and 0.525 were rejected (9.490 vs 10, 8.835 vs 8.33, 8.945 vs 8.42). 84 of 206 measured edits moved the rating by 3 or more tries, and only 49 moved toward the target. Examples: one spare less took 7.60 to 18.54; adding lockedPartners took 7.60 to 1.70.
Claude's 9 cloud-tuned v7/v8 rows: only 1 passed its own search check (206 af639e5f66952d0d, 7.31, skilled 4.42); the other 8 were offCurve. None of the 9 made the final 15.
TASK-02 (23:40): fill the 11 missing slots, keep the 15 fixed, re-rate near-misses with more campaigns. Superseded at 23:50 before it ran.

Origin of the 7-9-10 curve: Dennis 2026-11-04, 'we need to start at 200 now that players are further'; 175-199 stay as they are. Before that the 175-200 curve was on the g2.1 scale (about 3.3 to 4.5 at 199). On the human-g6.x family scale the hardest live levels sit around 7 (132: 7.05, 150: 6.2-6.9), so 7 at 200 meant 'start at the hardest live level'.

Origin of the current curve (TASK-03, 2026-11-04 23:39). Dennis: 'I think the first levels are too easy. Start the levels at 10 tries at 200.' Asked whether he meant family or himself: '1 [family 10 -> 13] and require the skilled bot to at least need 2.5-3 tries.' Family 10 at 200, 12 at 224, 13 at 225 (linear, about +0.083 per level), with 225 a +1 jump; skilled 2.5-6. Claude's own note to Dennis: 'on the bot's scale 132 and 150 sit at about 7, so 10-13 is above anything the family has played.' Dennis's follow-up: every board over 70 tiles (minimum 72), block shapes discouraged.

Task 03 hint list (from Codex's 1,537-board screen): recipes with high family medians were frozenGuards 15, clockOnTopLocked 15.6, keyToEscape 12.7, trayJuggleFrozen 12.7, dontGrab+lockedPartners 16.4. Low: lockedClock 1.3, deepKeys+iceChain 5.5, blindTwins+iceChain 5.5. predict.js (family rating from board make-up) had rank 0.59 in-sample. Its top quarter landed within 2.5 tries 20% of the time, against 8% for the bottom quarter.

TASK-04 (2026-11-05 01:45): skilled-bot fix. On clocks frozen or locked with the keys across the pile, the planner measured progress only by tiles on the clock and found no way in 90% of searches. Fix: count what the clock still needs. Two-island 212 went 11.7 to 2.15; Dennis's lab boards were off by 2.18, now 2.05; live levels unchanged. Dennis: 'it should be on if the measurements come out okay'. Same-board effect on v10 delivered boards: 210 2.27->2.95, 217 2.15->2.88, 225 2.08->3.45 (these 3 would fail the 2.5 floor on the old bot).

Task 03+04 result (v10): 13/26 qualified (200, 201, 202, 205, 210, 211, 212, 213, 217, 220, 222, 224, 225). Pool 4,231; screened 3,911; full ratings 777; quality checks 239; quality passes 47. 492 missed target by more than 0.5; 160 had seed gaps above 2. The journal had 510 edits, 212 of them moved 3 tries or more. 6 boards still over 6 skilled (locked or double-iced clocks: up to 20).

Dennis's round-2 lab verdicts (2026-11-05). 200: 5 tries, 'right', 3 stars, 'Shape is not the most fun. Its okay.' 217: 2 tries, 'easy', 4 stars, 'Very fun. Clock can be tighter. maybe do a -1 on clock for levels like this.' 225: 4 tries, 'right', 5 stars, 'Very fun clock seems good here. Can it be tighter? Not sure.' The Task 04 skilled bot matched him: 200 5.15 (he 5), 217 2.88 (he 2), 225 3.45 (he 4).

TASK-05 (2026-11-05 18:30): new skilled player = better of two styles (route worked back from the clock, or plain play), commit 3201e1e. Lab boards off by 1.93, live 1.05. A placement score from Dennis's lab quotes: decisive tiles between 15% and 60% of the solution; specials visible; at most 1 face-down tile on the way to clock/keys; spare 1 on tray-juggle levels; a temptation; pile shapes, no blobs. Fill the 13 missing slots.

Task 05 result (v11): 9/26, zero new qualifiers. 132 deals on 34 layouts (mean placement score 86.1); pool 1,002; full ratings 148; quality passes 11. The new skilled bot dropped 4 accepted boards under 2.5: 210 2.95->2.27, 217 2.88->2.15, 220 3.52->2.0, 225 3.45->2.08 (Dennis needed 4 tries on 225 and gave it 5 stars). 217 at spare 1 went to family 20 (capped). 18 of 20 proposed new layouts failed the originality search. Codex: 'This score did not predict expert challenge: many good-looking placements were too easy or had idle components.'

Hidden tiles drive most of the skilled difficulty on accepted boards. Skilled as-is vs all face-up: 200 5.15 vs 1.05; 202 4.55 vs 1.18; 205 3.42 vs 1.07; 211 3.33 vs 1.0; 212 3.4 vs 1.18; 222 2.7 vs 1.07; 224 5.75 vs 1.13. Only 213 (3.23 vs 2.88) is hard mainly by order. 201 is the reverse (5.42 vs 19.93). Task 07 later found the cause: a short-horizon planner flaw (canRelieve accepts any immediate relief and misses two waits sharing one later key gate), not the board.

Task 05 hidden-route audit of retained boards: hidden tiles on the clock/key route were 18 on 200, 13 on 202, 9 on 212, 5 on 224. That breaks Dennis's 'not blind digging' rule (at most 1), which applies only to new boards.

TASK-06 (2026-11-05 23:40, superseded and never run on its own). Asked for: Dennis's lab tries (if he won and rated 'right' or 'hard') to stand in for the skilled rating of that exact board (225 qualifies again at 4; 217 stays out); a skilled predictor fitted on the pools; steering steps that raise skilled more than family; big boards 210/220 first (lost on skilled 2.38 and 2.0); explain 201. Superseded by Dennis 23:27: 'I like all this work but I dont really want to play the levels. We want the designer to have tiny puzzle pieces / traps that it uses to design every level and knowing how hard the outcoming level generally will be.' The human-win rule was applied in Task 07 (v12 restored 225 with effective skilled 4).

My analysis of the handed-back pools: family vs skilled correlation r=0.155 (round 1, 90 boards), -0.038 (v10, 218), -0.327 (v11, 76). Seed 4711 vs 18427 correlation 0.76 / 0.83 / 0.71, median gap 0.9 / 0.98 / 1.18 tries, gap > 2 for 48/273, 160/777 and 28/148. Share of quality-checked boards under skilled 2.5: 59/90, 136/218, 62/76.

A recipe does not set difficulty. v10 family quartile ranges: iceLockClock 7.6-13.2, keysAcross+frozenGuards 9.0-13.4, clockOnTopLocked 8.9-12.8, trayJuggleFrozen 8.9-12.2. Skilled medians by recipe are mostly 1.1-2.7. The ones that reach the 2.5 floor are keysAcross+frozenGuards (3.33 in v10), frozenGuards+deepKeys (4.58) and deepKeys+iceChain (4.33), but these vary between rounds (keysAcross+frozenGuards 1.07 in v11).

keyFacts.fact: Slots were filled by over-producing and assigning, not by design. Only 2 of 15 (round 1) and 2 of 13 (v10) delivered boards sit in the slot their creation was authored for: for example, creation level-315 became 200 and level-313 became 225. The variants that reached the curve were almost all 'reveal/hide N covered pictures' or 'clock spare N'. In round 1's pool: reveal 153, hide 97, spare 93 of 418 candidates.

The steering journal (624 measured edits by v11) contradicts the 'lessons' given to Codex. Median factor and share of edits that went up/down by more than 10%: luck moment added x1.04 (31% up / 28% down); one ice softer x0.97 (46% softer); trap added deepKeys x1.42 (p10 0.22, p90 2.89); trap added lockedPartners x1.41; clock -n spare x1.15 (p90 1.82); clock moved later x0.40 and earlier x0.23 (both make it easier); relief swap x0.45. 253 of 624 edits moved the rating by 3 or more tries; median absolute change 1.84 tries.

Dennis's quotes behind the Task 05 placement rules (lab, before 200-225): 'frustrating cause the hard part is tray pressure at the very end to get the keys. Replace.'; 'the ending is annoying to finish'; 'The locks put you in the right direction otherwise you dont know where to go before the clock.'; 'I like easy looking shapes with hard problems'; 'Digging without seeing exactly where is not very engaging.'; 'too loose ... adds nothing'; 'I dont see how I can take the clock faster then this route'; 'Get rid of the blob levels'; 'I like the pile shape better then blobs'; 'More smartness in how traps are placed would be nice'.
Ratings in v12 (Task 07) after 13 extra fresh seeds: 3 of 13 diagnostic boards passed the independent check, but almost all also failed 'skilled too easy' (skilled 0.67-2.03 at family 10-12).

failedApproaches.approach: Random fresh deals on new layouts with a named recipe bolted on, then over-produce and screen (Tasks 01, 03).
failedApproaches.result: Yield 15/26 (round 1) and 13/26 (v10) from 2,100 and 4,231 candidates; about 20% of fully rated boards land within 0.5 of any target; assignment upper bound was 16 slots both times.
failedApproaches.whyFailed: Difficulty depends on where the pictures fall, not on the recipe: recipe quartile ranges span 4-6 tries. Slot-targeted construction does not work; only 2 of 15 and 2 of 13 boards landed in their authored slot.

failedApproaches.approach: Local steering / tuning with a journal of measured edits (moves.js), using 'reliable' steps: luck moment to make harder, one ice softer or half the ice to make softer, clock moved along the way, avoid adding traps.
failedApproaches.result: In round 1 none of the 9 Claude-tuned rows and few PC-tuned rows qualified; 49 of 206 edits moved toward the target. By v11, 253 of 624 edits were cliffs of 3 or more tries.
failedApproaches.whyFailed: Edit effects are not monotone and depend on context. The 'luck moment' median is x1.04, split evenly up and down. The 'traps make easier' lesson from the first 101 moves reversed with more data (deepKeys median x1.42). A single seed's noise (median gap about 1 try) is as large as most step effects.

failedApproaches.approach: Tuning with the same seeds used for acceptance (holdout seed 18427 reused).
failedApproaches.result: Winner's curse: tuned boards look on-curve but fail fresh seeds (round-1 210 pooled 8.1 vs fresh 7.2; 213 8.015 vs 10.53).
failedApproaches.whyFailed: Two 40-campaign seeds correlate only 0.71-0.83, so selecting on them overfits noise. The fix was a reserved seed 29717 for tuned rows.

failedApproaches.approach: Curve set from Dennis's own feel after playing (7 to 10 at 200 after round 1: 'the first levels are too easy').
failedApproaches.result: Target moved above anything the family has played (live hardest about 7 on the bot scale); most round-1 boards became unusable (1 of 15 fit the new curve).
failedApproaches.whyFailed: Dennis is the skilled player. His 'too easy' was largely about skilled difficulty (round-1 skilled 1.0-2.7), but the fix raised the family target. Raising family difficulty did not raise skilled difficulty (family-skilled r about 0); the result was family-hard, skilled-easy boards ('skilled too easy').
failedApproaches.source: README lines 607-614; TASK-03; my correlation analysis

failedApproaches.approach: A skilled floor of 2.5 measured by a skilled bot that kept changing (Task 04 planner fix, Task 05 better-of-two-styles).
failedApproaches.result: Qualifiers flipped in and out with bot versions: 3 v10 boards would fail on the old bot, then 4 accepted boards (210, 217, 220, 225) failed on the Task 05 bot. 225 went 3.45 to 2.08 although Dennis needed 4 tries and loved it.
failedApproaches.whyFailed: The skilled bot has policy blind spots: locked/frozen clocks, the 201 face-up paradox (5.42 vs 19.93), up to 20 on double-iced clocks. Its numbers are not stable enough to gate on near 2.5.

failedApproaches.approach: Smarter trap placement scored before bots by a hand-made 0-100 placement score from Dennis's quotes (Task 05).
failedApproaches.result: 132 deals, mean score 86.1, zero new qualifiers; 10 midgame-relay overlays, none passed.
failedApproaches.whyFailed: The score encodes what Dennis likes to see, not what makes a puzzle hard for a skilled player. High-scoring placements were too easy (skilled about 1) or had idle components. Codex: 'did not predict expert challenge'.

failedApproaches.approach: Adding connected support motifs (keyGuardIce, partnerRelay, thawRelay, midgameRelay) to existing recipes.
failedApproaches.result: Journal: keyGuardIce x1.00 (9/9 no change), partnerRelay x1.00; idleSupport failures.
failedApproaches.whyFailed: Added pieces mostly did not bite. Visible connected traps can still be strategically idle.

failedApproaches.approach: Clock spare -1 to make a fun easy level harder (Dennis's 217 request).
failedApproaches.result: 217 at spare 1: family 20 (capped), off the curve.
failedApproaches.whyFailed: The spare is a cliff knob (round 1: 7.60 to 18.54 for one spare less).

failedApproaches.approach: Fresh whole original layouts for every slot with strict originality (D4 overlap, no crops).
failedApproaches.result: Catalogue grew to 48 layouts, but in Task 05, 18 of 20 proposed new layouts failed the originality search.
failedApproaches.whyFailed: The space of distinct non-block shapes of 72-96 tiles is running out under the overlap rule; this becomes a supply bottleneck for 'all levels ahead'.

reliableFindings: The family bot rating of one board on one 40-campaign seed is noisy: seed-to-seed r = 0.71-0.83, median gap about 1 try, and 16-21% of boards differ by more than 2 tries. Any per-level tolerance below about ±1 needs more campaigns or more seeds (Dennis later approved ±1.0 per level, with every 5 consecutive levels within ±0.5).

Family difficulty and skilled difficulty are independent dimensions on these boards (r between -0.33 and +0.16). Traps that catch the family usually do not catch a planner. The design has to target skilled difficulty on its own, not hope it follows from family difficulty.

On the accepted boards the skilled difficulty comes mostly from hidden tiles: all face-up drops skilled from 2.3-5.75 to about 1.0-1.2 (except 213, 3.23 to 2.88). So 'hard for Dennis' currently means hidden information, which is exactly what Dennis says he does not want as the main difficulty ('Digging without seeing exactly where is not very engaging').
A recipe name does not set difficulty: a recipe's family rating varies 4-6 tries between quartiles, and skilled medians by recipe change between rounds.

Single-step edits are not reliably signed. Even supposedly safe edits have p10/p90 spanning both directions, and about 40% of edits are 3+ try cliffs. Small changes swinging a level from easy to near-impossible are confirmed by 624 measured edits.
The clock spare and the clock's position on the way are the strongest knobs, and they act as cliffs. Moving the clock earlier or later on the way usually makes a board much easier (x0.23 / x0.40).
Selection plus independent re-measurement works where steering fails: the qualifiers came from large pools assigned to whichever slot they fit, checked on a reserved seed.

The skilled bot's absolute number can match Dennis well on some boards (Task 04 bot: 200 5.15 vs 5, 217 2.88 vs 2, 225 3.45 vs 4) but shifts by 0.7-1.4 tries between bot versions, and it has known policy blind spots (locked/double-iced clocks rated up to 20; 201 face-up 19.93).

The gates kept by all tasks (special matters by ablation, losses at the traps >= 60%, at most 1 unrelieved dig, clock-first check, spare 1-3, valid stored solution through the real game, phone preview) were applied honestly; no gate was relaxed in Tasks 1-6.

Dennis's stated tastes are consistent across lab rounds: pile shapes, not blobs; a visible way that the specials point to; a clock that is tight but fair; difficulty in the early-to-middle part, not tray pressure at the end; not blind digging; a temptation at the decision point; 'easy looking shapes with hard problems'; fun matters more than exact difficulty (225: 4 tries, 5 stars).
openProblems: There is no way to build a board whose skilled difficulty comes from order and tray decisions rather than hidden tiles. 'Skilled too easy' (about 1.0-1.15 at family 10-12) was the main failure from v11 on and was never solved in Tasks 1-6.

The curve's scale is unclear. Family 10-13 at 200-225 is above the hardest live levels (about 7 on the same bot) and was set from Dennis's own skilled feel. Whether the family can actually take a jump from 199 to 10+ is unknown. No player data on 200+ exists yet.

No validated predictor of family or skilled difficulty from board structure: predict.js has rank 0.59 in-sample; the placement score did not predict; Task 06's skilled predictor was never built; the Task 07 composition model failed prospectively (MAE 7.64).

The skilled bot as judge is unstable across versions and has blind spots (locked/frozen-clock routes, the 201 face-up paradox from short-horizon relief logic). Gating on a 2.5 floor makes qualification depend on the bot version.
The family bot's own blind spots relative to real family players (people lose to the tray early, at 68-76% of the board left; the bot later, at 48%) are untested on 200+ boards.
Retained accepted boards (200, 202, 212) carry 9-18 hidden tiles on the clock/key route, against the 'at most 1' blind-dig rule. The legacy boards were never brought up to the new design rules.
Supply of original layouts: 18 of 20 new layout proposals failed originality in Task 05, so the strict D4-overlap originality rule may not scale to 'all levels ahead'.
How much Dennis's single play is worth as a rating (the Task 06 human-win override) is undecided beyond the exact boards he played; he does not want to playtest routinely.

recommendations: Treat family difficulty and skilled difficulty as two separate design axes and design each on purpose. In this data, raising one never raised the other.

Stop single-step steering toward a 0.5 band. Over-generate and select, then confirm on reserved seeds; that is what actually filled slots. Budget for it: about 5-6 full ratings per qualified level under the old gates, much more with the skilled floor.

Set tolerance from measured noise (median seed gap about 1 try): judge levels in windows (Dennis approved ±1 per level, ±0.5 per 5-level average) rather than chasing per-level precision the meter cannot give.

Before building, make the 'difficulty source' explicit and check it without bots: skilled as-is vs all face-up is a cheap, decisive diagnostic. Require that most skilled difficulty survives all face-up (order/tray puzzle), so that hidden tiles are not the main difficulty, as Dennis asked.

Do not let a single skilled-bot version gate near its floor. Pin the bot version per batch, and keep Dennis's real lab tries (won and rated 'right' or 'hard') as the override; fix known planner blind spots (short-horizon relief, locked/double-iced clocks) before using it to judge boards.

Re-examine the curve with real data: 10-13 family tries at 200-225 sits above every live level on the same bot (hardest about 7). Consider a smoother hand-off from 199, and check against player data once 200+ is played.
Avoid cliff knobs (clock spare, clock position on the way) as fine-tuning; if used, use them only as coarse tier selectors with re-measurement.

Plan for layout supply: the strict D4 originality rule is starting to block new shapes (18 of 20 failed); define what 'original' must mean for hundreds of future levels (for example, a new puzzle on a reused layout family).

result.summary:
Across five tasks from 5 to 7 Nov 2026, Codex tested every way so far of making difficulty something you can compose or steer. Each one failed when tested in advance on new boards. Along the way the work kept finding that part of the "difficulty" is really bot blind spots.

Task 07 built 16 named trap pieces (pieces.js) and measured them on 8 calm bases: 384 placements, 358 measured. Alone, almost every piece was worth x1.00 tries for both bots. Only the clock and its route mattered: clock depth 2 with spare 1 gave x2.16 with an IQR of 1.52-11.97, and clockWay share 0.3 gave x16.6. A ridge composition model failed its prospective test: family MAE 7.64, 0 of 12 qualified. On target-band boards it did worse than simply predicting the median. One concrete cliff: swapping a single piece moved a board from 11.55 to 16.98, and raising its spare from 1 to 3 then moved it to 7.28.

Task 08 widened the tolerance to +-1 per level, plus a mean within +-0.5 over every 5-level window (Dennis approved). Reusing the existing pools then reached 16/26 levels. The frame-first conditional model failed its registered test 0/12, with skilled spanning only 1.00-2.17. The same frame (share 0.20, depth 4, spare 2) rated family 2.39 to 19.24 depending on the base. Frames create family pressure only: skilled stayed at 1.00-1.20 even when family hit the 20 cap.

Task 09 dropped predictive models. It filled 20/26 by brute force: 5,856 pool boards, 1,549 full ratings, 76 quality passes. 36% of the 746 journaled single changes moved difficulty by 3 or more tries. The best recipes reached both bands on only 13-41% of paired boards. The missing slots (208, 210, 215, 216, 217, 221) failed mainly on "skilled too easy" and on seed disagreement.

Builder v2 passed its construction gate: 135/150 builds, every intent proven, no idle specials. In the clock-spare study, spare 1 to 3 made 18 of 20 boards easier.

Task 10 tested the knobs on the same puzzle. Moves with 3 tiles waiting, luck and designed traps were worth about 0 tries. Only spare worked: -0.71 per extra move, -1.13 without frozenGuards, which had an 11.2-try cliff. Of 200 range-grid boards, exactly 1 landed in both bands. The additive table missed held-out cells by a median of 3.78 family and 2.69 skilled tries. Different builder seeds for the same brief spread up to 17 tries. The pilot hit 0/11, and every pilot build failed the readable-objective rule.

Task 11 (still running) found and fixed a big family-bot blind spot. The released family profile forgets on every retry that a tile it saw was a key. The candidate `family-key-memory-v1` restores that knowledge. It passed all inherited real-player fit gates (family live MAE 2.081 to 2.079, planner unchanged). It lowered 117 hidden-key Task 10 boards by a mean of 6.18 tries (97 easier, 10 harder). On boards with no key showing at the start, the median fell from 19.76 to 9.24 and the count at 18+ from 77 to 16 of 88. So much of the "hidden keys make it brutal" story was the bot, not the puzzle.

The re-rating also moved kept levels. Only 15 of the 20 kept levels stay within +-1: 205 goes 10.4 to 2.4, 213 goes 11.0 to 4.4 and 223 goes 12.2 to 18.3. The yardstick itself was part of the problem.

The 60-board error study found no structural difference between bands: route length and real forks are both a median of 15 on easy, middle and hard boards. What differs is the bots' behaviour. On hard boards the family bot picks a losing move at a live fork 23.1% of the time versus 5.5% on easy boards. Its first error comes earlier (move 5.5 versus 9), and the loss shows later: about 10 removals after the error versus 5 (corrected figures; the per-band table in ERROR-PROFILES.md still shows the pre-correction numbers). On hard boards it also repeats known losing moves: 543 repeats in tries 6-20, with 1 win in 711 attempts.

The way ladder is a cliff, not a slope, in 5 of 6 story/layout pairs, under both the old and the new bot. Changing the way length rebuilds the puzzle, and neighbouring lengths swing by up to 18 tries.

Task 11 has not been handed back as done. All 852 re-rating measurements, the follow-up phases and the 185-test regression suite finished (the re-rate script crashed on a summary step after its last measurement). The hand-back generator has uncommitted edits, and the candidate bot is not merged or adopted.

reliableFindings: Clock spare is the only monotone same-puzzle control: about -0.7 to -1.1 family tries per extra move (23/24 or 20/21 boards in the expected direction). Small skilled effect (-0.2 to -0.3). Not exact: frozenGuards had an 11-17 try cliff, and some boards do not respond.
Picture-level knobs (three waiting, luck/hidden on the way, designed traps as currently built) do not move ratings (about 0 tries). Do not rely on them for difficulty.

Difficulty depends on the whole board's structure and jumps. Rebuilding (way length, builder seed, swapping one piece) can swing 10-18 tries. Only exact same-puzzle transforms (spare) behave smoothly.

The family bot (old version) forgets key identity between tries, which inflates hidden-key boards by about 6 tries on average. The fix passes all real-player fit gates. Any rating, recipe hit rate or 'hidden keys make it hard' finding from the old bot is suspect on key boards.

Real fork counts and route length do not separate easy from brutal boards (both 15). Brutal boards differ in how tempting the losing choices are (family losing-pick rate 23% vs 5.5%) and in delayed punishment (about 10 removals vs 5). The most common first error is taking an attractive free face-up pair too early (400/928).
Unique-order openings are not the cause of brutality on Task 10 boards (0/16 had a single winning opening).
Frame pressure alone produces family difficulty with skilled about 1.0. Skilled 2.5-6 needs genuine decisions or luck, not just a tight clock.
Bot disagreements show up as large rating jumps under information changes (all face-up making the planner worse). Use such counterfactuals as blind-spot detectors.
Early stopping with a 4-try margin after 20 campaigns is calibrated (1.72% false stops) and saves about 48% of family CPU (old bot; must be recalibrated for the new bot).
The readable-objective rule (keys and route visible) eliminated every v2 pilot board; builder v3 now enforces readability by default.
openProblems: Adopting family-key-memory-v1: Claude must review and merge it. With it, the 200-225 batch drops to 15/20 within +-1 (205, 213 too easy; 223 at 18.3 too hard; 224 and 206 drift). Release decisions and Dennis's OK are needed before re-curving levels.
Why 223 (iceLockClock) became harder (12.2 to 18.3) and 10 of 117 hidden-key boards got harder with better key memory: not explained.

Second family-bot blind spot, measured but not fixed: on hard boards in tries 6-20, 543 known-picture losing moves are repeated (1 win in 711 attempts). There is no memory of 'this move lost last time'. Whether a human would also keep failing is unmeasured (no human plays on the research boards).
Planner blind spots, not fixed: canRelieve's short horizon on shared key gates (201 all face-up 19.93); frozen keys not seen as keys; peek/action representation artifact when all tiles are face up.
There is still no control that raises skilled into 2.5-6 reliably; skilled is about 1 on most built boards.

No structural descriptor yet predicts the cliffs; the proposed controls (key reveal timing, a tempting pair versus a readable safe plan, delay before a bad choice is punished) are untested as controls.
The new bot needs its own early-stop recalibration; old thresholds do not carry over.

Task 11 is not formally done: the hand-back generator has uncommitted edits; summary-for-dennis.md and BUILDER-CONTROLS.md are not yet published to the results folder; Gemini's G2 fast mode is not yet merged.
The 6 missing slots (208, 210 big, 215, 216, 217, 221) are still empty; with the new bot there are now more holes (205, 213, 223, possibly 206, 224).

recommendations: Fix the yardstick before designing to it. Adopt or decide on family-key-memory-v1 (it passes all fit gates), then hunt the next blind spot: the repeated known losing move (543 repeats in late tries on hard boards). Re-derive every hit rate, band and descriptor association with the new bot; old 'hidden keys = brutal' numbers mostly reflect the bot.
Do not build another predictive composition model or additive table: four generations failed in advance (MAE 3.8-7.6). Treat the bots as the judge and build a process that tolerates cliffs.

For fine-tuning, use only exact same-puzzle transforms. Clock spare is the one proven smooth control (about -1 family try per move). Any change that rebuilds the puzzle (way length, piece swap, builder seed) is a new board and must be re-rated.

Design decisions, not pressure. Brutal and easy boards have the same fork counts; the difference is tempting wrong choices (especially a free face-up pair taken early) and how late the punishment comes. Make the trap explicit and readable: a visible tempting pair against a visible safe plan, with a short, controlled delay before a bad choice is punished, proven by the engine.

Use the information-change counterfactual (all face up, key memory on/off, frozen key unfrozen) as an automatic blind-spot check. Reject boards whose rating swings a lot when only information changes, because that difficulty is the bot's, not the puzzle's.
Keep readability (keys and route visible), no frozen keys on the critical path, and visible-key timing as design and clarity rules, not as difficulty knobs.
Skilled 2.5-6 cannot be produced by family-style pressure (frames give skilled about 1). It needs real choices or controlled luck; measure what actually raises the planner before relying on it.

Recalibrate early stopping for the new bot, then use generate-many, screen cheaply and confirm fully. Expect low hit rates per recipe (13-41% joint at best on the old bot); plan CPU accordingly (one heavy job at a time).
Get human ground truth on a few boards where the bots disagree: Codex's 3 playable examples (9001-9003), and 205/213/223 old vs new, so Dennis can say which bot reads them correctly.

recommendations: Use the zero-drift fast meter as soon as Gemini commits it and Claude merges it: it speeds up ratings without moving any rating. Before relying on it, settle the meter.js conflict with Codex's BOT_VERSIONS change. Decide which bot version is the reference before proving zero drift again.

Do not build the level process around the GPU proxy as a band filter. At most use it as an easy-floor cut (score >= ~5.2 keeps ~95% of in-band boards and drops ~57% of easy ones). It cannot reject too-hard boards, which is the builder's main failure.

Use the exact GPU or CPU simple-playout kernels for structural questions that need many random playouts: how many move orders reach the clock in time, how much a deal's face luck matters, whether a single non-obvious order exists. A cheap bot can measure these exactly, which makes them a better design signal than a proxy for the family bot.

Treat 'keys visible at the start' and 'clock route length vs spare' as first-class design variables. The proxy's calibrated key memory went to ~0, its false positives were long-route and hidden-key boards, and the builder found hidden keys cause 88% of 18+ ratings. This contradicts Gemini's bot-designer rule of burying keys.

Require held-out validation for any rating or design claim: Gemini's in-sample results were overturned several times (bot-designer 60% -> 1/6, g5 anchors, g1 test counts). Fitting thresholds to anchor levels (150, 132) does not generalize.

Keep in mind that bot ratings match humans only weakly on live levels (Spearman about 0.15-0.39 against Dennis's targets). A process that steers difficulty only by family-bot expectedTries inherits these blind spots. Plan for human feedback (Dennis's verdicts, live play data) as the outer calibration loop.
Coordinate CPU use: Gemini's 20-worker bench was running at 08:15 while Codex Task 11 was active. Any new task to Gemini should say when CPU benchmarks are allowed.

result.summary: This folder holds the record of "builder v2/v3", the attempt (2026-11-06/07) to replace "random deal + bolted-on traps + factory tuning" with a constructive builder (tools/builder/builder.js plus stories.js, engine.js and gate.js). It works in three steps: pick one of 10 stories (keysFarSide, keysOnIsland, clockInSight, iceLockClock, lockBeside, frozenGuards, chainReaction, roomInTrayLocked, roomInTrayFrozen, deepClock), place the roles, then plan a dig to the clock, with targets for way length, tray pressure ('three'), luck, hiddenOnWay, traps and spare. Phase 1 (descriptors-report.md) measured 194 bot-free board descriptors on 1,989 rated boards. On real historical boards every descriptor is weak. Family: best rho about 0.19-0.20 (singles parked on the clock way, moves with 3 waiting, way share/length, decision points), and it roughly halves within one factory batch (0.07-0.14). Skilled: best rho 0.33 (luck moments, i.e. a face-down tile uncovered while 2+ wait; within-batch 0.27) and face-down tiles taken on the way (0.30, within 0.31). On the gate band (family 9-14), no single measure beats balanced accuracy 0.61. Only on purpose-built experiments (528 boards with almost no face-down tiles) are the links strong for the family: moves with 3 waiting rho 0.73, way length 0.66, has-clock 0.74. Phase 2 (gate) went from failing (v1: idle specials 55, unproven intents, slow builds) to passing (codex-final: 135/150 builds, every intent proven, 0 idle specials, all under 5 s). But the gate only certifies that boards are honest and match their brief. It says nothing about difficulty, and the built boards were far calmer than the real 200-225 levels (median 1 vs 5 moves with 3 waiting; median way 8 vs 14). Phase 3 (Codex Task 10, knobs-v1) is the key negative result. On the same puzzle (opts.keep), tray-pressure, luck and designed-trap knobs move the bot ratings by about 0 tries (medians +0.14, 0.00, 0.00, -0.04). Only clock spare works: 23/24 in the expected direction, about -0.71 to -1.13 family tries per move, but with an 11.2-try cliff on frozenGuards. Across puzzles the rating distribution is bimodal: of 347 rated boards, 152 are at 6 or below, 145 at 18 or above, and only 7 in 10-13. Only 1 board of 347 hit both bands. Repeating the same brief with builder seeds 1/2/3 gave family spreads up to 17 tries. An additive story+knob model missed held-out cells by a median 3.78 family / 2.69 skilled tries, and the pilot hit 0/11 first-checks with no new qualified level. why-hard-claude.md then found the main cause of the jump: whether the keys are visible at the start (0 keys showing: median 19.8, 88% at 18+; 2 showing: 6.3). A causal ladder (keysShown 2/1/0) confirmed hidden keys raise the rating in 5/6 pairs but not as a clean step, because every request rebuilds a different puzzle. Codex Task 11 (in progress, read from its running note) found that the reference family bot has no retry key-identity memory (only 24/643 next-try openings moved toward a key it had already seen). A key-memory bot candidate passed the human-fit gates, and under it 54/61 hidden-key boards so far got easier. So a large part of the 20-try cliff is a bot blind spot, not difficulty a person would feel. An uncommitted 'cone' analysis by another session (research/cone.json, 148 Task 11 boards) gives the strongest single predictor seen so far: way singles outside the family bot's 'attraction cone' (rho 0.42 family / 0.49 skilled; 0 outside: median 4.6; 2 outside: median 17.1). That points to bot sight and attention, not board 'pressure', as what the ratings actually measure. The cc-builder-loop is set up only (round 0). Its goal is controls that move ratings predictably for family 10-13 / skilled 2.5-6.

reliableFindings: Clock spare is the only knob that is reliable on the same puzzle: about -0.7 to -1.1 family tries per extra move (23/24, 20/21 excluding frozen keys), a weak skilled effect (-0.2 to -0.3). It is a fine-tuning control, not a conversion formula, and does not work with frozen keys.
No clock means no difficulty (family about 1.0 try). The family bot loses almost entirely to the clock (99% of losses on a 20-try board are the clock).

Family and skilled difficulty come from different sources. Family: clock way length and tray at 3 on it (strong only on clean experiments, rho 0.66-0.73). Skilled: face-down tiles uncovered while 2+ wait (luck) plus losing choices with the way length held fixed. A board can be hard for one and easy for the other.

Builder-made difficulty is bimodal (347 boards: 152 at <=6, 145 at >=18, 7 in 10-13), and construction seed alone can swing a brief from 3 to 20 tries. Any process must measure every final board, not predict from the brief.

Visibility of the objective dominates: hidden keys at the start push the family bot to the 20 cap (88% at 18+). Part of this is a bot blind spot (no retry key memory); a key-memory bot candidate passed the human fit and makes most hidden-key boards easier.

Bot ratings partly measure bot attention: way moves outside the family bot's attraction cone are the strongest descriptor seen (rho 0.42/0.49, uncommitted). The all-face-up ablation raising skilled 1.1 -> 19.4 shows bot artifacts can dominate ratings.
engine.js (peek pairs, game clock timing) is the correct reference for winnable / fewest moves / traps; strict tools are only safe witnesses.
Gate infrastructure is solid and fast: proven intents, honest clock (winnable at k, lost at k-1), no idle specials, under 5 s, 157 tests. It can serve as the honesty filter in a new process.
Real 200-225 qualified levels are long and tight (way median 14, 3-waiting median 5, luck median 1) compared with builder output (way 8-10, 3-waiting 1-2, luck 0).
Same-puzzle comparisons (opts.keep, knobs.js clock-only transform) plus frozen plans and fixed seeds are a sound experimental method; across-puzzle comparisons are confounded.
openProblems: No control yet gives a slope in difficulty inside 10-13 family; the middle band is almost empty for builder boards (7/347).

How much of the 18-20 cliff is real human difficulty and how much is bot blind spots (key memory, visible-role key routing, cone horizon 3)? Task 11 final results with the key-memory bot are pending (852 re-ratings in progress).
Whether the rating bot should switch to family-key-memory-v1. It passed the fit, but only 15/20 kept levels stay within ±1 under it, so the curve itself may shift.

Readable boards (hiddenOnWay 0) remove the main skilled lever (luck), and 5 of 6 missing slots failed partly on 'skilled too easy'. What raises skilled difficulty to 2.5-6 while staying readable is unknown; candidates are real choices under pressure and decision traps with the way length held fixed (rho 0.28).
Way-length ladder (Task 11 part 2, 6 pairs, ways 9-15, spare 1/2): slope or cliff? Measured, but the conclusion is not yet reported.
The cone descriptor is uncommitted and untested as a builder control: can the builder place a fixed number of way singles outside the cone and get a monotone rating change?
Game-side issues waiting for Dennis's OK: validSolution and the hint solver (layouts.js solve) do not know peek pairs; a builder level relying on a peek pair has no strict witness.
chainReaction and iceLockClock build poorly at long ways; trayRoom 2 builds 62.5%; traps exist only with spare 1.

recommendations: Do not design around brief parameters that predict the rating: every attempt (descriptors, knobs, additive model) failed. Use a generate-many, measure-each, select process, and use descriptors only as cheap pre-filters.

Fix the rating instrument before steering by it. Decide on the key-memory family bot (passed the fit), and check the other blind spots (visible-role key routing, cone horizon, all-face-up skilled artifact). Otherwise the cliff to 20 is partly measuring the bot.

Use visibility/attention structure as the primary difficulty axis: keys shown at the start (0/1/2), moves until the objective shows, and way singles outside the bot's cone (rho about 0.4-0.5). These are the only levers with large effects; test them same-puzzle (opts.keep style) so the puzzle does not change under the knob.
Use clock spare (about -1 family try per move) only as the final fine-tuning step after a structure lands within about 2 tries of target, and never on frozen-key boards.
Keep the gate (honest clock, proven intents, no idle specials, readable, >=72 tiles, engine with peek pairs) as a hard honesty filter; it is fast and trustworthy.

Treat family and skilled as separate targets with separate levers. Skilled under readability needs a lever other than hidden luck: decision traps / deep losing choices with the way length held fixed are the best remaining candidate (rho 0.20-0.28).

Expect a bimodal rating per structure. Build per-structure families with a small slope (e.g. one hidden key revealed after N moves) and measure the slope, rather than hoping a global knob interpolates.
Measure several construction seeds per brief: seed spread can be 17 tries, so a single build says little about the brief.
Prefer stories with visible objectives (keys in sight, a visible ice guard instead of frozen keys); drop frozenGuards and chainReaction in their current form.

result.area: Builder and factory code (level-builder worktree: source/tools/builder/, source/tools/factory/, meter and bot API)
result.summary:
The builder (source/tools/builder/builder.js, 838 lines, "Builder v2/v3", Claude 2026-11-06/07) builds a board backwards from a brief {layout|shape|tiles, story, stage, frame{spare,way,depth}, targets{trayRoom,three,luck,hiddenOnWay,maxDown,traps,keysShown}, seed}. It runs five stages. (1) placeRoles picks the clock, locks, keys and ice on one of 48 fixed layouts (analysis/builder/data/layouts.json), following one of 10 stories in stories.js. (2) planDig works the dig P back from the clock, and `necessary()` finds the dig tiles that every way to the clock must take. (3) placePictures pairs pictures along P. Two necessary tiles get "orphan" twins buried under holders, so the tray is forced to the requested cap; the rest are paired greedily. An optional decision trap is a free face-up off-dig pair. (4) placeDown places the face-down tiles. (5) The clock is set to the engine's real fewest moves plus spare, idle specials are pruned, and every intent is proven. Only then is a board returned with a design card ("bites" sentences).

engine.js is the exact-rules proof tool. It covers peek pairs, the clock checked after the whole action, ice, locks and the 4-slot tray. It offers winnable, clockShortest, classify (win/lose/unknown per legal move, with depth capped at 12), traps, replay and kindOf. It caches by board contents, and when a budget runs out it answers 'unknown', never a loss. Builds are fast: the codex-final gate built 135 of 150 (90%), every one fully proven with no idle specials, at a median of 17 ms (p90 542 ms, max 3.8 s). Wall time was 35 s for 150 builds on 2 jobs.

The bot meter (factory/meter.js createMeter().measure(board,{setting:'family'|'planner', runs:20, seeds:2, seed})) is a content-addressed disk cache. Its key combines the board, the settings and a fingerprint of the bot's whole require() source closure. A production family rating pools 80 campaigns (seeds 4711 and 18427, 40 each), capped at 20 tries. The skilled rating is the planner, taking the better of its route and plain styles at 40 campaigns each. A family campaign costs about 250 ms of CPU, so one family rating is about 20 s on one core. The planner costs 440-1050 ms per campaign, so about 35-85 s per board. Gemini's zero-drift fast path (G2 part A: 100 boards, 0 drift, about 5.5x for family) exists but is not merged into wip/level-builder yet.

The decisive finding is that the builder hits its numbers on paper but does not control difficulty. In Task 10 (1,041 measurements, 347 boards), the picture-level knobs moved ratings by about 0 tries on the same puzzle: three-waiting +2 gave +0.14 family, luck 0.00, traps 0.00/-0.04. Only clock spare was monotone: 23/24 pairs, median -0.71 family tries per move, or -1.13 with frozenGuards left out. The rating instead jumps with the structure: way length, key visibility at the start, frozen keys, and whether the right move is unobvious under forced pressure. Only 1 of 347 boards landed in both bands. The pilot hit 0 of 11. The additive model missed held-out cells by 3.78 family / 2.63 skilled tries. The GPU proxy (G2 part B) reaches only Spearman about 0.50 and fails its bar.

The core structural weakness: every request, every seed and every target change builds a new puzzle, because placeRoles and planDig are driven by the rng. Two examples: keysShown 2/1/0 on keysFarSide L20 gave 20 / 2.0 / 16.4, and seeds 1/2/3 of one brief gave 19.3 / 6.9 / 19.1. The same-puzzle path (opts.keep) exists only for the picture-level knobs that did nothing. The design also puts pressure where there are no choices: the greedy pairing forces every move. Its traps are full-information solver proofs that ignore what a player can see, while the bots, and probably people, lose to information (hidden keys, moves outside the family bot's 3-blocker cone).

The reliable parts are worth keeping as building blocks: the engine, knobs.clockSpare, the gate's static checks, placement_score.readable (Dennis's rule), tileVisibility, the meter cache and fingerprint discipline, opts.keep, and loop/busy.js. The factory (101 files) is the older generation: deal-then-steer (design_*, steer_design), the trap composer, measured pieces and frames (pieces-v1 family MAE 7.64; frames-v2 0/12 prospective hits), and Task 9 empirical_* production (20/26 kept levels). Its prediction models all failed. Its gates (originality, preview_check, trap_supports, final seed 29717) are what qualified the live levels.

keyFacts.fact: Build pipeline: placeRoles (story geometry: clock, locks, keys, ice) -> trimThawLocks -> planDig (dig P worked back from the clock) -> chooseHolders -> necessary() (order-free: pinning the tile makes the clock unreachable) -> picturesFor/placePictures (orphans with buried twins force the tray to the cap; greedy pairing along P; optional trap = a free face-up off-dig pair) -> placeDown -> fewest() via E.clockShortest -> replan if a shorter way exists -> prune idle specials -> prove(). Up to 16 attempts, hard stop 4.5 s, soft stop 2.5 s; only all-proven boards are returned.

10 stories: keysFarSide, keysOnIsland (needs 2 peaks; fits 19 layouts), clockInSight, iceLockClock, lockBeside, frozenGuards, chainReaction, roomInTrayLocked, roomInTrayFrozen, deepClock. A story is a role spec only (clockDepth, clockLock, clockIce, coverLock, keys far/deep/near/island, keyCover, keyIce, coverPartners). Pictures are not part of a story.

Brief contract: trayRoom 0/1/2 = exactly 3/2/1 waiting on the witness to the clock. hiddenOnWay is a minimum, maxDown a cap (default 0.3). three, luck and frame.way are within 1. Luck needs trayRoom 0. Covered-partner stories need trayRoom 0 or 1. frame.share and trapDepth return unsupportedTarget. 72-96 tiles enforced. v3 adds targets.keysShown (0/1/2) and requires a readable objective unless hiddenOnWay >= 2.

Engine API: game(design,{strict}), start, legal, step (null = immediate loss), winnable(g,s,{nodes,ms}) -> win/lose/unknown, clockShortest -> {k,path} (real fewest moves with peek pairs), classify (per legal move win/lose/unknown + depth capped at 12), traps(g,path), replay, flatten, kindOf. DEF budgets: win 2e6 nodes/10 s, move 1e5/300 ms. The cache is keyed by a JSON signature of the content, after Codex found stale-cache bugs. The solver knows all faces.

Peek pairs made recorded spare wrong on 5 of the 18 qualified 200-225 boards (202: 2->4, 203: 3->4, 204: 1->3, 222: 3->5, 225: 1->3). Hard.validSolution and the hint solver (layouts.js solve) still do not know peek pairs; fixing them needs Dennis's OK.

Gate codex-final: 135/150 builds (90%), 46/50 briefs, median 17 ms, p90 542 ms, max 3,813 ms for successes; every intent proven, 0 idle specials, all static checks clean. Weak spots: chainReaction 7/15, trayRoom 2 15/24, spare 1 39/51.

Task 10 same-puzzle knobs (median family change per request): three+2 +0.14, three+4 0.00, luck+1 0.00, luck+2 0.00, traps1 0.00, traps2 -0.04, spare+1 -0.71 (23/24 in the right direction). Excluding frozenGuards, spare is 20/21 at -1.13 family / -0.32 skilled. frozenGuards showed an 11.2-try cliff.

Task 10 range: 292 requests, 200 built and rated, 1 board in both bands (family 10-13, skilled 2.5-6). Per-story family medians: keysFarSide 5.99, keysOnIsland 18.92, clockInSight 20.00, iceLockClock 9.61, lockBeside 5.54, frozenGuards 18.58, chainReaction 20.00, roomInTrayLocked 4.29, roomInTrayFrozen 2.98, deepClock 4.08. Additive model held-out error: 3.78 family / 2.63 skilled tries. Pilot: 0/11 first-check hits; every new whole-layout pilot build failed the readable-objective rule.
Seed instability on one brief (keysFarSide, way 14, three 5, luck 1): seeds 1/2/3 gave family 19.26 / 6.93 / 19.09. Way 10 -> 14 on keysFarSide jumps from about 3 to about 19-20.

Key visibility: with 0 keys showing at the start, family median 19.8 (88% at 18+); 1 key 13.0; 2 keys 6.3. The keysShown ladder (one seed, 10 campaigns only) gave keysFarSide L7 2.0/3.7/20, keysFarSide L20 20/2.0/16.4, iceLockClock L7 20/20/20. Each keysShown request builds a different puzzle.

Frozen keys: removing their ice at the same exact spare moved family 20.00 -> 3.40 and skilled 9.10 -> 1.00. The planner builds keyTiles from visible key roles, and a frozen key shows as ice (a hidden-role blind spot). AllFaceUp raised skilled 1.13 -> 19.38: a policy/peek-action artifact.

Codex Task 11 (in progress): the released family bot has NO retryKeyIdentityMemory, while the 'dennis' setting does. Of 643 next-try key opportunities, only 24 (3.7%) went first toward a previously seen key. A candidate bot human-g6.3-key-memory-candidate1 (fingerprint d362e85f...) passed every human-fit gate (family-weighted MAE 2.0812 -> 2.0794) and improved 54/61 hidden-key boards so far. With it, only 15/20 kept 200-225 levels stay within +/-1, against 20/20 on the reference bot.

Task 11: all 16 brutal both-keys-visible Task 10 openings have at least 2 proved winning first actions (0 uniquely winning). Unique-safe states later on the way occur on easy boards too (median 4 easy vs 5 brutal), so 'unique state present' is not a difficulty control by itself.

Meter: createMeter({bot, cacheDir, fingerprint}).measure(board, {setting, runs:20, seeds:2, seed:4711, capture}). Cache key = sha256(fingerprint, canonical board without solution/gold, settings). The fingerprint hashes the bot's whole require() closure plus G51_* env. Invalid or censored results are never cached. Only explicit FAMILY_CACHE_MIGRATIONS are allowed (current fingerprint f3285928..., planner-only revisions). Cache dir: source/build/factory-cache.

Rating protocol: family = 80 campaigns (seeds 4711 and 18427, 40 each), 20-try cap. Tuned rows also need final seed 29717 within 0.5 of target and a seed spread <= 2. Planner (skilled) = better of route/plain styles, 40 campaigns each. Curve (Dennis 2026-11-04): 200 at 10 family tries rising to 13 at 225, skilled at least 2.5 (band 2.5-6). Curve tolerance +/-1 per level, and every 5-level window averages within +/-0.5.

Rating cost: family about 236-275 ms per campaign (only 14% is decide(); 84-85% is environment overhead: generator patching, structuredClone per tap, verify() replay, visibility), so one 80-campaign rating is about 20 s on one core. Planner route style 440-635 ms per campaign, plain 1,053 ms on 96 tiles. Fast path estimate: about 3.3 s single-core, about 0.25 s/board throughput on 20 threads for family.

G2 part A zero-drift fast path: 100 boards, driftCount 0, 575,627 family and 383,222 planner moves checked, fingerprint 4cf0b4c7... Not yet merged into wip/level-builder (head 0e9d6479). G2 part B GPU proxy: held-out Spearman about 0.50 family; at 90% in-band keep it discards only 42% of clearly-out boards and 2% of the hard >= 18 ones. It fails the bar (90% keep / 50% discard).

Tests: builder test_builder 10, test_describe 5, test_engine 15, test_gate 3, test_knobs 2, test_task10* 10, test_reach 6. Factory: 107 test() calls across 19 files (trap_composer 19, factory 14, candidates 13, empirical 12...). Codex reported 157-168 builder+factory tests passing.

reliableFindings: engine.js is a trustworthy exact-rules oracle (peek pairs, clock after the action, ice, locks, tray). It never claims a loss it could not prove, and its cache compares board contents. Use it for honest clocks, winnability and per-move classification.

knobs.clockSpare (only clock.n changes; the full witness is replayed) is the one monotone control: 23/24 pairs in the right direction, median -0.71 family tries per extra move (-1.13 excluding frozenGuards), skilled -0.21 to -0.32. It is a fine-tuning knob, not a conversion formula. Effects vary by board, and some boards do not respond.

Construction is cheap (median about 17-30 ms, p90 under 1 s), and every returned board has a proven witness, an honest clock and no idle specials. The bottleneck is entirely the bot ratings (about 20 s family plus 35-85 s planner per board on one core today).

Difficulty for the bots is set by structure and information, not by tray-pressure counts: way length (about 10 moves gives 2-6 tries; 14+ often gives 20), whether the keys and objective are visible at the start, frozen or hidden roles, and moves outside the family bot's 3-deep blocker cone.

Same-brief, different-seed builds are different puzzles with ratings from about 7 to about 19. Any process that needs a predictable rating must hold the puzzle fixed and tune only proven monotone controls, or measure every candidate.

Readability (placement_score.readable: objective in sight, at most 1 face-down tile on the route, no face-down clock, key or lock) is Dennis's rule and is now a required builder intent. It interacts strongly with difficulty: hidden objectives produce 20-try cliffs.

Bot ratings depend on the bot version: the key-memory candidate (which passes the human fits) moves 5 of 20 kept 200-225 levels outside +/-1. The curve scale is tied to a fingerprint, and the meter enforces that (no silent cache reuse).
The 20-try cap censors the hard end: many boards sit at 18-20, so there is no gradient there to steer by.
openProblems: Whether the 18-20 ratings on hidden-key boards are real human difficulty or a bot memory blind spot. The family bot lacks retryKeyIdentityMemory, and the candidate fix is being re-rated in Task 11 (852 measurements running).

There is no control that moves difficulty steadily within a fixed puzzle, other than clock spare. What creates real choices (several plausible moves, one wrong, visible to a player) has not been built or measured as a knob.

The builder has no way to vary one structural parameter (way length, key visibility, key distance) while keeping the rest of the puzzle fixed. opts.keep freezes the roles and the dig, so it cannot change them.

What spreads the both-keys-visible boards from 3 to 20 (iceLockClock, lockBeside, keysFarSide L20). Task 11 found 0 uniquely winning openings among 16 brutal ones, so 'unique forced order' is not confirmed as the general cause.

Time budgets make builds non-deterministic under CPU load. Budgets are wall-clock based (DEADLINE, softMs 2.5 s, hardMs 4.5 s, within()), so the same brief and seed can return a different board on a busy, shared PC.
Release blocker: builder levels whose clock relies on a peek pair have no strict witness for Hard.validSolution, and the hint solver does not know peek pairs. Both need Dennis's OK to change.
G2 fast path (zero drift, about 5x) is not merged yet. Its fingerprint and migration must be registered and reconciled with Codex's new key-memory bot version.
The 20-try cap removes information at the hard end; the curve targets 10-13 sit near the area where ratings saturate.
Only 48 fixed layouts and 10 stories. The originality rules (shared coordinates under 75%, block shapes discouraged, 72+ tiles) limit reuse across hundreds of future levels.
frame.share and trapDepth are unimplemented. Covered-clock stories cannot lengthen a dig on purpose; they only pick a clock whose dig happens to be long enough.

recommendations: Stop treating each request as a new puzzle. Build a level from a fixed puzzle (layout, roles, dig) and adjust it only with proven monotone controls (clock spare first, then any new control that passes a same-puzzle paired test). Extend opts.keep so that one structural variable can change while everything else stays frozen.

Measure the structural knobs that actually move ratings (way length in single steps, keys shown, moves until both keys show, key distance) on fixed puzzles before relying on them. Task 11's way ladder (way 9-15 at spare 1/2) is the first data. Do not reuse the picture-level knobs (three, luck, traps): about 0 effect.

Design difficulty as real choices on the critical route (visible, plausible alternatives where one loses), checked with engine.classify plus the visibility model (tileVisibility and the cone), not as forced pressure. A trap should be proven against what the player can see, not only with full-information winnable.

Ban by construction the causes of unintended difficulty: hidden or frozen keys, objectives not in sight (already the readable intent), moves outside the bot's cone that a person would only find by chance, and unique non-obvious orders. Report each on the card so a 20 can be explained.

Pin the bot version before calibrating any curve. Settle Codex's key-memory candidate and Gemini's fast path first (both change or keep fingerprints), because the kept 20 levels move from 20/20 to 15/20 within +/-1 under the candidate.
Make builds deterministic: replace wall-clock budgets (DEADLINE, softMs, hardMs) with node budgets, or record the attempt, so a brief plus a seed reproduces the same board on a busy shared PC.

Use the cheap, solid parts as the base of the new process: engine.js, gate.js checks, knobs.clockSpare, placement_score.readable, meter.js cache discipline, the factory's originality/preview/final-seed gates and busy.js. Treat the factory's prediction models (predict, pieces, frames, GPU proxy) as failed.

Budget for rating cost: about 1-2 CPU-minutes per board today (about 5x less with G2 merged). Use Task 10's calibrated early stopping (20-campaign prefix, 1.7% false stops) for screening, but qualify only on the full protocol.

Housekeeping before relying on the suite: test_reach.js (uncommitted in level-builder) needs the missing reach.js, and research/*.js hard-code /home/claude/repo-oma paths and use 10-campaign ratings, so treat their numbers as indicative only.

result.summary: Main is now at 1.65, released 2026-11-06 (level replays), not 1.64. levels-hard.js has not changed since 2026-10-16 (1.54). Levels come from three sources. Levels 1-50 and 52 are dealt live on each phone by layouts.js forLevel/makeDeal, tuned to the old botWinRate. Levels 51 and 53-69 are fixed boards in levels-early.js (Gerda's recorded boards, with 51 and 53 swapped). Levels 70-269 come from HARD_LEVELS in levels-hard.js: 200 packed rows, v8, aspect 1.6, reorderFrom 92, cycleFrom 150. Past 269 the game reuses 150-269, mirrored and with shuffled pictures, so the content never runs out. Grandma (OmaHanny) has her own care track, dealt live for her screen. It never uses the table; from 119 her rules move towards the family's. Every board from 70 to 269 has the same make-up: 72-96 tiles, about 40% face-down, 36 picture kinds, usually 10-12 ice and 6-7 locks with one key pair, and a clock from 80. There are no exact towers, 5-24 tiles are free at the start (median 12), and big boards (more than 88 tiles) sit only on every tenth level. Every difficulty setting has been at its maximum since about level 100, so only the picture arrangement and the clock can change difficulty. All 106-269 boards are one generator's output (hard.js make, release 1.47, 2026-10-12, picking the pile with the fewest free tiles). Their pictures were re-tuned in 1.48 and remade in 1.53, and the boards were reordered whole in 1.52 and again in 1.54. As a result 122 of the 164 piles are at least 90% the same as an earlier one, and 14 are identical. The targets on paper always flattened out: 1.47/1.48 aimed for a strong-bot first-try rate of 30% from 150 onward, and 1.53 aimed for 40% from 170 to 269. Only the 1.54 reorder (two fitted personal bots, five-point ease bands, smoothing) produces a rising curve on paper: model Dennis 48%->34%, Mrs. Doubtfire 36%->17% from the 100s to the 180s. I re-read Firebase plays/ (read only) on 2026-11-07. Real results do not follow that curve. Dennis wins about 64-70% of first tries and needs a median of 1 try in every band from 120 to 199, against 35-41% predicted. Mrs. Doubtfire's band averages match the model (43/27/19% vs 41/29/22%). Gerda's median tries stay flat at 4-6. Per level, the reorder's prediction has no link to real tries (rank correlation -0.03 for Dennis, -0.06 for Gerda, 0.13 for Mrs. Doubtfire), and neither does the stored chance. The real spikes (91, 132, 149, 150, 144, 188, 196) are single boards that one or two players found brutal: Gerda needed 68-82 tries on 91/132/149/150 and 37 on 188, and Dennis needed 9 on 196. The players hardly agree on which levels are hard (rank 0.03-0.18). The packed chances (fields 8 and 9) are only written to the start log as pr/pm. Nothing in the game or the dashboard reads them, and they predict nothing per level. Dennis won 199 and started level 200 on 2026-11-04 on the old 1.54 board. A way to replace boards was built only on origin/wip/release-1.63: ship_batch.js, HARD_LEVELS.revisions with a per-range save generation, and test exemptions. It was never released, and main has none of it.

reliableFindings: The live table 70-269 is one generator's output (hard.js make, 1.47) with pictures re-tuned and the boards reordered several times. All structural difficulty settings (40% face-down, 36 kinds, 10-12 ice, 6-7 locks, clock) have been at their maximum since about level 100, so nothing structural is left to raise difficulty further. Difficulty from there on comes only from the picture arrangement and the clock tightness.

Every official curve flattened out: 30% strong from 150 in 1.47/1.48, 40% strong from 170 in 1.53. The rising curve exists only in the 1.54 personal-bot predictions, and real play does not follow it for Dennis (flat about 65% first try) or Gerda (flat median 4-6 tries). Mrs. Doubtfire's averages fall slowly as predicted.
Per level, no measure so far (stored chances, the 1.54 personal bots) ranks real difficulty. Band averages are the most any model has matched (Mrs. Doubtfire's yes, Dennis's only at 92-119).

Real difficulty is dominated by a few spike boards that one or two players found brutal (Gerda 68-82 tries on 91/132/149/150, Mrs. Doubtfire 39 on 144, Dennis 9 on 196). Those are what feel like near-impossible jumps. The players disagree on most other levels (rank 0.03-0.18).

Clocks were loose historically (1.45: 27-76 moves) and were cut to the route plus 1-3 spare moves. Losing early to the clock (132) and squeezes in the middle of the board (150) are the two documented real hard patterns. 57% of human losses happen before the clock is taken.

New boards replace existing rows in the 70-269 table: the table length is fixed at 200 by tests, and 270+ automatically cycle 150-269. A replaced row in 150-269 therefore also changes the cycled levels beyond 269.

Shipping new boards needs the revisions/designVersion mechanism (only on origin/wip/release-1.63), test exemptions (t_clocks clock.n<=19 and spare 1-3; t_reorder_honest hash checks; big boards only on lv%10==0), Dennis's approval, and release.py from a clean main with the full suite passing.

Real tries must be counted up to the first win only, with restarts counted as losses, and only on the current board (match the tile count and the version: 1.54+ for 92+). There is a rage tail, so cap at 12-20.
openProblems: Dennis has already started level 200 on the old 1.54 board (2026-11-04 18:50), and Gerda is at 191 and Mrs. Doubtfire at 176. A 200-225 batch has to ship before they go further; replacing a level they have started restarts their saved game. RULES.levels.blockedFrom could hold levels but has never been used.

The 200+ target (family bot 10 -> 13 tries) is above every live level on the bot's scale (132 and 150 score about 7). Moving from the flat, mostly easy 175-199 (Dennis 1 try on 18 of 25) to that would be exactly the kind of jump the user wants to avoid. The bridge from 199 has not been designed.

No meter has been shown to rank real per-level difficulty. Whether any can, given that the players disagree (best possible rank about 0.5), is unknown, so a curve can only be checked as averages over windows.
How much Dennis has improved over time (first try 0.55 -> 0.70) versus the levels getting easier is not separated. The 1.54 personal bots used fits from 2026-10-16 and were not re-fitted.

Grandma's care track is a separate, live-dealt level system with the old bot and no stored boards. Dennis wants her eventually at family level ('maybe ~100 levels on'), and no process covers her levels.
What makes the real spikes hard is only partly known (132 = clock opening, 150 = mid-board squeeze, 91/149 = hidden tiles). There is no rule that predicts a spike before players meet it.
Pile repetition in 175-269 (many piles at least 90% alike) will keep coming back through the 270+ cycle unless 150-269 are replaced.

recommendations: Treat the live 92-199 'curve' as flat and noisy, not as a rising baseline. For Dennis it is about 65% first try and median 1 try, and for Gerda a median of 4-6 tries, with rare spikes. Design the 200+ start from real numbers for 175-199, not from the model curves, and plan an explicit ramp from there instead of jumping to family 10.
Judge the curve on windows (5-10 levels) and per-player averages. Per level, use real data only for spike detection after release, because no meter ranks single levels and the players disagree.

Make spikes deliberate and rare (named 'peak' levels with a known, readable cause such as the 132 clock opening or the 150 mid-board squeeze). Avoid accidental spikes from hidden tiles (91/149) and bot blind spots. Real spikes cost Gerda 68-82 tries.

Ship ahead of the players. Dennis is already on 200. Use RULES.levels.blockedFrom, or build batches before players arrive, so replacements do not reset saves on levels in progress. Port the revisions/designVersion and test-exemption code from origin/wip/release-1.63 into the release path early.
Plan for 270+: rows 150-269 feed the endless cycle, so replacing 226-269 (and the repetitive 150-199 piles) also fixes what players see beyond 269.

Do not reuse the packed fields 8/9 or Hard.target as difficulty truth. Store the new meter's label in ratingModels (as ship_batch.js does) and keep the shipped boards' measurements in source/analysis/.

Re-measure players' current skill (Dennis has improved to 0.64-0.70 first try) before setting the curve. Keep Dennis's weighting (2 x Dennis + Gerda + 2 x Mrs. Doubtfire) and the 'tries until first win, capped' rule as the real yardstick.
Decide on grandma's care track separately. It is generated live with the old bot and is not covered by any table process.

result.area: What real players experience: tries, win rates, where they get stuck, how players differ, how well the bots predict them, and what "fun but challenging" looks like in the data
result.summary: The real players who matter for difficulty are Dennis (Dennisisdebeste, pmuy78xu6tsths9, the skilled player), Mrs. Doubtfire (pmv16kj3jr35750) and Gerda (pmv6yhzz3x9oxs8). Grandma (OmaHanny, pmuy4wmdp17hbws) plays her own gentler "care" track with tray rescue and adaptive ease. The analyses so far cover levels 85-174 from Firebase plays/ and replays/, mostly exported between 2026-11-01 and 11-02. For 175-199 there is only a three-line note in the factory README; I found no data file or cached export for it. On live 150-174 Dennis wins 64% on the first try (median 1). From 157 to 173 he won 15 of 17 levels first try (no record for 166). Mrs. Doubtfire wins 20% first try, median 3, mean 4.6 (156: 15 tries, 162: 10, 150: 21). Gerda's cached data stops at 154, and her extremes are huge: 82 needed 103 tries, 91 68, 132 73, 149 76, 150 82. The real family difficulty is very spiky. On the family-weighted yardstick ((2xDennis + Gerda + 2xMrsD)/5, capped at 20) the median is 3.4 and the quartiles are 2.2/4.6. Eleven of 66 levels are at 6 or more, and neighbours jump by 4 to 12 (131 2.6 -> 132 13.6 -> 133 1.0; 149 6.0 -> 150 13.2 -> 151 3.4). The players hardly agree on which levels are hard (rank 0.17, 0.18 and 0.06 between pairs). A fitted per-level difficulty barely improves held-out prediction (log-likelihood per try -0.4854 with levels vs -0.4934 without). People lose early: tray losses come with a median of 65-71% of the board still left, and about 27% of losses are to the clock. Casual players hit walls at the clock openings: PUK lost about 25 tries to the clock on 80 with 86 of 96 tiles left, and has 15 losses and no win on 82 (11 of them clock losses at 68 of 76 left). Grandma was at 72% first try through 119, then dropped to 25% at 120-128 once the 1.61 "catch-up" ramp began, and was stuck on 128 when her data ends (2026-10-27). The most important finding for the design: the inherited bot fit gates are no better than a constant guess. Family-weighted MAE is 2.08 against 1.73 for always guessing the median 3.4. Planner live MAE is 1.009 against 0.797 for always guessing 1. Dennis's actual live-try MAE is 0.933 against 0.722 for always guessing 1. Lab MAE is 1.945 (1.366 censor-aware) against 1.58 for always guessing 2. They are regression guards, not evidence of prediction. The reference family bot reads old live levels at about 0.78x the real yardstick (mean 3.11 vs 3.97, rank 0.36). It rates only 3 of 66 live levels at 7 or more (124 15.0, 121 7.1, 132 7.05; 150 6.9). So the current 200-225 target of 10-13 family-bot tries sits above every level the family has played except one: harder than 132 and 150, the two most-struggled levels. On boards Dennis played in the lab and factory the bots order better (g2.1 Spearman 0.79; planner lab rank about 0.68). "Fun but challenging" has a clear signature in Dennis's ratings. Wins in 4-6 tries average 4.1 stars (8 boards), 2-3 tries 3.1, first-try wins 2.3 ("way too easy"). Unwon or late-squeeze boards get 1-2 stars. His good boards have losses early (60-78 tiles left), a goal he can read ("the locks put you in the right direction") and an "easy looking shape with a hard problem".

How people lose (85-174, tries up to first win): Dennis 16 clock / 28 tray / 19 restart; Gerda 192 / 501 / 15; MrsD 61 / 158 / 5. Clock is 25-27% of losses for all three. Median tiles left at a tray loss: Dennis 68%, Gerda 71%, MrsD 65% of the board. The bots lose later (about 48% left).

Level 150: the clock is almost always taken, then the tray fills mid-board (tiles left at loss: Dennis 58, Gerda 72, MrsD 54 of 96). The bot loses later (42 left) and wins about 1 in 2.7 tries vs Gerda 1 in 81.

Casual players hit walls at the clock: PUK lost about 25 tries to the clock on level 80 (86 of 96 tiles left, 11-53 s per try) and on 82 has 15 losses and no win (11 clock losses at 67-68 of 76 left) as of 11-03. Mama stopped at 44 (10-12) and Rashmi at 53 (10-19) while still winning, so those stops are not difficulty walls.

Grandma's track is designed for about 90% first-time clears, adaptive ease, tray rescue and a helper. Her real first-try rate was 70-92% through 119, then 25% from 120 to 128 (121: 3, 123: 5, 124: 9, 127: 9 tries, 128 not won after 4) once the catch-up to family face-down share and deal targets began (119->143, release 1.61).

reliableFindings: The family's real difficulty concentrates on a few spike levels (91, 132, 150, then 144, 89, 122, 149, 156), and adjacent levels swing 1 -> 13 tries. The three players agree on those few and on little else.

People lose early: tray losses with about two-thirds of the board left, and about a quarter of losses to the clock (132, 80, 82: opening clock puzzles). Clock openings with a 1-move margin are the main wall for weaker players (Gerda 103 tries on 82; PUK stuck on 82; Gerda 54 of 70 losses on 132 to the clock).

Dennis is far stronger than the family: 64% first try at 150-174 vs MrsD 20% and Gerda about 10%. 160-174 were nearly all first-try wins for him, so the live 150-199 stretch is easy for Dennis and hard, with spikes, for the family.
Gerda does not quit: she keeps retrying, sometimes for 70-100 tries, with faster rage taps late. Capping per-player counts (12 or 20) is needed before averaging.
Per-level tries of a single person are mostly chance; use the curve (windows of levels) and multi-player pooling, not single-level promises. Dennis approved ±1 per level and ±0.5 per 5-level window.

Dennis's fun signature: wins in 4-6 tries (about 4 stars), early losses, a goal he can see (clock and locks in view), easy-looking shape with a hard order problem, a clock that matters but whose route he can find. Disliked: first-try wins, blind digging, a squeeze at the very end, a clock too loose or impossibly tight, a special that adds nothing.
