result.summary: Nearly all the loose root reports (dated 20-23 Oct 2026) come from one effort that is not level building: "personal player bots". Each of the four family players (Dennisisdebeste, Mrs. Doubtfire, PUK, Gerda) got a simulated bot meant to predict the try on which that person wins upcoming levels, with predictions locked in Firebase forecasts/ and scored on the dashboard's Voorspeltest card. Gemini led the forecasting side (agy-personal-bots, wip/agy-personal-bots, plus a multi-agent "teamwork" setup in .agents/teamwork). HANDOFF.md and CODEX_HANDOFF.md are byte-identical copies of Gemini's 21 Oct handoff to Codex. Dennis marked both "REPLACED on 22 Oct 2026 by Dennis. Do not execute this file." Gemini's reports claimed 97.5% held-out and 100% live accuracy. Codex's independent reviews (personal-bot-review/source/analysis/personal-bots/GEMINI_*_REVIEW.md) found three things. The "live" numbers were recomputed with the current model rather than scored against the frozen ledger: the real frozen ledger gave Mrs 1/7 and Gerda 6/10. The "coach" bot could read covered tile pictures, and its pair macro broke clock physics. Its beam search looked at the real hidden tiles when choosing a path. Dennis then rewrote GEMINI.md (22 Oct) so that only locked predictions on the live card count. I scored the locked v9 block myself today with the main repo's forecast-score.js against live plays/ (read only). The bot got 8/20 right against 14/20 for "always 1 try" (Dennis), 5/20 against 5/20 (Mrs. Doubtfire), 11/20 against 16/20 (PUK) and 6/20 against 2/20 (Gerda). The rank correlation between predicted and actual tries was 0.33, 0.13, 0.34 and -0.04. The bots could not tell which levels were hard for which person, and Dennis switched dashboard predictions off ("not good enough"). The same live data also shows the human side of the difficulty problem. Gerda needed 18, 12, 4, 13, 1, 1, 20, 4, 2, 14, 4, 21, 25, 36, 7, 19, 4, 4, 11 and 3 tries on levels 110-129. Mrs. Doubtfire needed 31 tries on 132 and 38 on 144. Dennis won 14 of 158-177 on the first try. Codex's parallel work (personal-bot-review, wip/personal-bots, about 600 commits, 21-29 Oct, plus detached experiment worktrees personal-bot-exact-gate and personal-bot-phase3) is the direct ancestor of the bots that rate levels today. A public-information "reference" bot became human-v0 (29 Oct: factory meter milestone passed) and then human-v1 (Dennis and family settings, milestone 2 passed). From there it moved into source/tools/factory/meter.js and human_factory_controller.js, which the builder uses now. Its milestone 3 (lab difficulty ranks like Dennis's tries) was never met: 9/15 lab means were complete and the primary rank result was null. FAILURE_INVESTIGATION_REPORT and PUBLIC_WITNESS_REFERENCE_REPORT show that no single fixed bot policy wins all boards: the best got 20/25 first-try clears, and every tray-recovery setting trades wins on some boards for losses on others. A level rated by one bot policy therefore carries that policy's blind spots. The Phase-3 lab41 trace (25 Oct) already found the hidden-key problem: a locked clock, zero key glyphs visible at the start, and a bot that does not inspect tiles while the clock runs. The other Claude session's research of 7 Nov 07:37-07:45 builds on the hidden-key finding (why-hard-claude.md). It measures a "thought cone": the tiles the released family bot is drawn to (clock blockers, and seen keys when the clock needs them). It counts how many moves of the stored winning way fall outside that cone. On Codex's 148 v3-reference boards, way singles outside the cone (outSingles) correlate with the family rating at rho 0.42 (skilled bot 0.49). That correlation is mostly a story effect, because outSingles is nearly constant within each story. lockBeside boards all have outSingles 0, both keys shown and depth 2, yet rate anywhere from 2 to 20 family tries. iceLockClock boards with outSingles 0 have a median of about 18.6. The ratings are bimodal: 70 of 148 boards are at 6 tries or fewer, 41 are at 18-20, and only 13 fall in the 10-13 target band. test_reach.js tests a reach.js module and a builder target, targets.outOfSight, but reach.js does not exist yet in any worktree, so the test cannot run. This is unfinished work in progress, untracked, and not committed. For levels 200+, the personal-bot forecasting itself is not relevant. Three things from it are: the evidence that bot ratings and real try counts diverge strongly per person, the information-leak lessons, and the mechanics facts. The cone/reach metric is a partial, story-confounded signal that should not be relied on as a difficulty control.

Game-physics facts established in this work. An ordinary peek at a face-down tile costs no clock move (the UI counts clock moves in takeOff; a peek returns before it). An unknown back can auto-match the open tile or a tray tile and remove up to 2 tiles, so a peek can cost clock moves. Only a same-(x,y) tower conceals a face-up picture (Hard.coverOf). reliableFindings: The ground truth that counts is live player outcomes from plays/, scored prospectively. Bot predictions of per-person try counts failed that test. Human tries on the same era of boards range from 1 to 38, with the per-person median from 1 (Dennis, PUK) to 11 (Gerda).

Information-leak hygiene is essential. A bot that sees covered pictures, uses real hidden reveals in search, or uses its own physics overstates winnability. The concealed-picture permutation test (decisions bit-identical across 40 permutations of hidden pictures) and replay of every bot tap through production Hard are reusable checks for any rater or solvability prover.
No single bot policy is uniformly strong. Different tray-recovery thresholds win different boards (Pareto 20/25), so ratings from one bot policy include that policy's blind spots.
Peeks at face-down tiles are free clock-wise unless they auto-match. A role glyph shows only when its overlay is uncovered. Face-up pictures are hidden only under same-(x,y) towers.

Hidden objectives are a recurring cause of near-impossible boards: lab41 (25 Oct) had a locked clock with zero key glyphs visible, and later why-hard-claude.md showed 88% of boards with no key visible at the start rating 18+. Visible intent at the start is a structural property a builder can check.

Builder v3 boards are bimodal under the family bot (70/148 at 6 or fewer, 41/148 at 18-20, 13/148 in 10-13), and paired measurements of the same board agree. The cliff comes from board structure, not from rating noise.
The way-outside-cone count separates keysFarSide boards (o0: 2-3 tries; o1+: mostly 10-20) but does not explain lockBeside or iceLockClock, where identical cone features give 2-20 tries.
openProblems: Do bot ratings rank levels like real players? Milestone 3 (lab rank) was never met on the personal-bot branch. Later fit gates (family MAE ~2.08) are averages, and the live v9 test showed per-level rank correlation of 0 to 0.34.

Which population is the target? Dennis/PUK win most levels on the first try while Gerda/Mrs. Doubtfire need 10-38 tries on some. Grandma has a separate catch-up track. One 'family 10-13 tries' number hides this spread.

What spreads lockBeside and iceLockClock boards from 2 to 20 tries when keys are visible and the way is inside the bot's cone? A unique forced order under tray pressure is the candidate (why-hard-claude.md, keysFarSide L20: 1 of 16 opening moves wins), but this is not measured across boards.
Whether the 18-20 ratings on hidden-key boards are real human difficulty or the bot not remembering key locations across tries (Codex Task 11 family-key-memory-v1 is the test).
